section.title: The LORD's Lawsuit and What He Requires
section.sectionRationale: After the summit of the Bethlehem Ruler, Micah returns to the courtroom. The LORD summons the mountains as witnesses and brings a covenant lawsuit against His people: what have I done to weary you? He rehearses His saving acts, exposes the emptiness of religion offered without a changed heart, and gives the famous summary of true religion in 6:8. The chapter then reads the verdict over a city full of dishonest scales and violence.
section.thesis: The God who redeemed His people has a righteous case against their ingratitude and injustice; He does not want mountains of sacrifice but justice, mercy, and a humble walk with Himself, and where these are refused He justly sentences a corrupt society to futility.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the covenant lawsuit in which God recalls His redemption and asks what He has done wrong (1-5); what the LORD actually requires, over against costly ritual, namely to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly (6-8); and the verdict against a city of dishonest gain and violence (9-16).

units.label: The covenant lawsuit
units.note: plead your case before the mountains

verses.text: Hear now what the LORD says: “Arise, plead your case before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice.
Hear, O mountains, the LORD’s {{rib|indictment}}, you enduring foundations of the earth. For the LORD has a case against His people, and He will argue it against Israel:
‘My people, what have I done to you? Testify against Me how I have wearied you!
For I brought you up from the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery. I sent Moses before you, as well as Aaron and Miriam.
My people, remember what Balak king of Moab counseled and what Balaam son of Beor answered. Remember your journey from Shittim to Gilgal, so that you may acknowledge the righteousness of the LORD.’”

units.label: What the LORD requires
units.note: do justice, love mercy, walk humbly

verses.text: With what shall I come before the LORD when I bow before the God on high? Should I come to Him with burnt offerings, with year-old calves?
Would the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, with ten thousand rivers of oil? Shall I present my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?
He has shown you, O man, what is good. And what does the LORD require of you but to act {{mishpat|justly}}, to love {{chesed|mercy}}, and to {{tsana|walk humbly}} with your God?

units.label: The verdict on a corrupt city

verses.text: The voice of the LORD calls out to the city (and it is sound wisdom to fear Your name): “Heed the rod and the One who ordained it.
Can I forget any longer, O house of the wicked, the treasures of wickedness and the short ephah, which is accursed?
Can I excuse dishonest scales or bags of false weights?
For the wealthy of the city are full of violence, and its residents speak lies; their tongues are deceitful in their mouths.
Therefore I am striking you severely, to ruin you because of your sins.
You will eat but not be satisfied, and your hunger will remain with you. What you acquire, you will not preserve; and what you save, I will give to the sword.
You will sow but not reap; you will press olives but not anoint yourselves with oil; you will tread grapes but not drink the wine.

You have kept the statutes of Omri and all the practices of Ahab’s house; you have followed their counsel. Therefore I will make you a desolation, and your inhabitants an object of contempt; you will bear the scorn of the nations.”

rib.gloss: A legal dispute, controversy, or lawsuit. The prophets picture the covenant relationship as a court case: the LORD, the wronged party, summons creation itself as witness and brings formal charges against His people for breaking the covenant. It is a lawsuit born of love, meant not merely to condemn but to bring the guilty to acknowledge the truth and return.

mishpat.gloss: Justice, right judgment, the fair ordering of life that gives each person their due. To do mishpat is not a feeling but action: treating others rightly, defending the weak, refusing dishonest gain. God requires that His redeemed people mirror His own just character in how they live with one another.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast love, covenant loyalty, mercy that keeps faith. It is the very kindness God shows His people, and He asks them to love it, not merely perform it. To love chesed is to delight in showing loyal, merciful kindness to others because one has received it from God; the same word crowns the book at 7:18 and 7:20.

tsana.gloss: To be humble, modest, lowly. The phrase to walk humbly with your God describes a whole life lived in modest, dependent step with the LORD, neither proud before Him nor self-reliant. Justice and mercy toward others flow from this lowly, trusting walk with God Himself.

basic.context: Micah imagines a courtroom. God calls the mountains and hills as witnesses and puts His own people on trial, yet He begins not by listing their sins but by asking, my people, what have I done to you? He reminds them how He rescued them from Egypt and carried them through the wilderness. Then comes the heart of the chapter: the people ask what offering could satisfy God, piling up calves, rams, rivers of oil, even their own children, and Micah answers that God has already shown them what is good, to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with Him. The chapter ends with the sentence on a city that cheats with false weights and is full of violence.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a covenant lawsuit, a form the prophets use to confront a people who have broken faith with their Redeemer. Micah 6:8 is not a way to earn salvation by good behavior; it is the shape of life God has always wanted from people He has already redeemed by grace. Verses 6 and 7 are not endorsing child sacrifice but exposing the absurd lengths of a heart that will offer anything except itself. The closing verses describe judgment, not a rule to follow.
basic.originalLanguages: God brings a riv, a lawsuit, against His people. What He requires is summed up in three phrases: mishpat, justice, doing what is right by others; chesed, loyal, merciful covenant love, the very kindness of God; and to walk humbly, from a root meaning lowly and modest, in daily dependence on God. The same chesed that God asks for here returns at the end of the book as the chesed God Himself shows in pardoning sin.
basic.typology: The covenant lawsuit points ahead to the greater judgment, where humanity has no answer to God's just charge. The impossible offerings of verse 7, even a firstborn for sin, find their true and only sufficient answer in the Father who gives His own firstborn Son. And the humble walk with God is embodied perfectly in Jesus, who alone did justice, loved mercy, and walked in lowly obedience.
basic.christ: No pile of sacrifices could ever cover sin; the question of verse 6 hangs unanswered until Christ. He is the one who fulfilled Micah 6:8 flawlessly, and He is the firstborn given for our transgression that verse 7 gropes toward. At the cross God's just lawsuit against His people is answered, not by our offerings, but by His Son, so that mercy and justice meet.
basic.god: God is the just Judge who has a real case against sin, but He is also the wounded Redeemer who pleads, what have I done to you? He does not delight in ritual for its own sake; He wants justice, mercy, and a humble heart. He is patient, rehearsing His past kindness to move His people to return, yet holy enough to sentence dishonest gain and violence.
basic.crossReferences: Micah 6:8 stands with Hosea 6:6, I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and with Jesus in Matthew 23:23 on justice, mercy, and faithfulness. Psalm 51:16-17 and 1 Samuel 15:22 teach that God wants the heart, not mere offerings. Hebrews 10 shows the sacrifices could never take away sin, which Christ alone does.
basic.oneStory: The God who redeemed His people from Egypt now stands as their judge, showing that no amount of religion can substitute for a life of justice, mercy, and humble trust. But the lawsuit no sinner can answer is answered in Christ, the firstborn given for us, who lived the life God requires and bore the sentence we deserved.

context.literary:
The chapter is built as a courtroom drama in three acts, and the voices change. In verses 1 to 5 the prophet relays the LORD's summons and the LORD's own speech: the mountains and hills are called as the court, and God stands as both plaintiff and the one wronged. Verses 6 to 8 are the voice of the people, or of a representative worshiper, asking how to answer, and a calm reply that ends the series of questions. Verses 9 to 16 return to the LORD's voice for the charge, the evidence and the sentence.

The central movement is an escalating list that breaks off. The worshiper begins with a burnt offering and a year-old calf, moves to thousands of rams, then to ten thousand rivers of oil, and finally to the firstborn child. Each step is bigger than the last, and the sequence exposes the logic of bargaining: if the price is not met, raise it. Verse 8 answers in a different register altogether. It has no price and no quantity, only three short clauses, and it begins 'He has shown you.' The answer has been available all along.

The last section matches the first. Where the opening of the chapter asked 'what have I done to you?', verses 9 to 16 supply the answer in specific sins: the short ephah, false weights, violence among the wealthy, lying tongues. The curses of verses 14 and 15 then come in a pattern of three, eat without being satisfied, sow without reaping, press without anointing, each a pair of verbs in which the second cancels the first. The final verse names the dynasty the people have copied, the house of Ahab, and so closes the case on a historical note.
context.historical:
Micah's world was richer and harder than the courtroom language suggests. The eighth century brought commercial growth to Judah, and with it the means to cheat. The ephah was the standard dry measure, and a short ephah meant selling less than the buyer paid for; false weights in the bag did the same with silver. Amos describes merchants impatient for the Sabbath to end so they can reduce the ephah and cheat with dishonest scales, Amos 8:5. Behind such practices stood an economy that took the land and the harvests of the poor, as Micah 2:2 had said.

The frantic questions of verses 6 and 7 reflect a religious climate in which sacrifice was abundant and ethics were optional. Child sacrifice was not a figure of speech in Judah. Ahaz, a king in Micah's own lifetime according to the book's opening, 'sacrificed his son in the fire,' 2 Kings 16:3, and Manasseh did the same, 2 Kings 21:6. The question 'Shall I present my firstborn?' touches a real and horrifying practice among the nations, which the LORD said never entered His mind, Jeremiah 7:31.

The history recalled in verses 4 and 5 is selective and deliberate. Moses, Aaron and Miriam are the three leaders of the exodus, and Miriam's presence is remarkable, since she is named as a prophetess in Exodus 15:20. Balak and Balaam stand for the occasion when the LORD turned a hired curse into blessing, Numbers 22:5 to 6 and 23:8. The journey from Shittim to Gilgal moves from the last camp east of the Jordan, Numbers 25:1, to the first camp in the land, Joshua 4:19.

The statutes of Omri and the house of Ahab were a byword. Omri founded the northern capital at Samaria, and Ahab 'did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him,' 1 Kings 16:30, setting up an altar and a pole for Baal and Asherah. His seizure of Naboth's vineyard, 1 Kings 21, is the pattern of what Micah 2:2 condemns.
context.canonical:
Verse 8 is among the most quoted lines in the Old Testament, but it is not a lone statement. Deuteronomy 10:12 to 13 asks what the LORD requires of Israel in terms of fearing, walking, loving and serving. Hosea 6:6, a generation earlier, has the LORD say 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice.' Isaiah 1:11 to 17 lists the sacrifices and festivals God cannot endure and ends with 'learn to do right; seek justice.' Samuel told Saul that obedience is better than sacrifice, 1 Samuel 15:22, and the psalmist confesses that the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit, Psalm 51:16 to 17.

The lawsuit form belongs to the prophets in general. Hosea 4:1 says that the LORD has a case against the people of the land, Isaiah 1:2 calls heaven and earth to listen, and Jeremiah 2:9 uses the same verb, 'I will contend with you.' The call to heaven and earth as witnesses goes back to the covenant in Deuteronomy 4:26 and 32:1, so Micah is acting on the terms of the covenant itself. The curses of verses 14 and 15 are those of Leviticus 26:26 and Deuteronomy 28:38 to 40.

In the New Testament Jesus cites Hosea's line twice, Matthew 9:13 and 12:7, and says the Pharisees tithe herbs while neglecting justice, mercy and faithfulness, Matthew 23:23, and 'justice and the love of God,' Luke 11:42. A scribe who says that love for God and neighbor is more than all burnt offerings is told he is not far from the kingdom, Mark 12:33 to 34. Hebrews takes the argument to its end, where Christ comes to do God's will in place of sacrifices God did not desire, Hebrews 10:5 to 9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Micah wanted his hearers to experience the force of a charge before they were offered an answer. The opening is deliberately uncomfortable: the LORD asks what He has done to wear them out, and the people have no reply. The recital of Egypt, the leaders He sent and the saving acts at Balaam and the Jordan is evidence in a case, and the point of it is that His record is without fault.

The worshiper's questions in verses 6 and 7 show the heart of the problem as Micah saw it. The people are willing to give a great deal, up to their own children, so long as it can be settled with a transaction. What they will not do is change how they trade, judge and speak. Micah's reply in verse 8 removes the price tag from religion: God has already told them what is good, and what He wants is a life that expresses His own character toward neighbors.

The last section is meant to make the application concrete. Whatever 'justice' means, it includes honest scales and a truthful tongue, and the leaders are named as the ones who fall under the curse. Micah was not giving a mood but a program, and the sentence of verse 16 tells his hearers where the road of Omri and Ahab ends.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The lawsuit and its verdict record a historical dealing with Judah, and the curses of verses 14 and 15 are not a formula that guarantees a bad harvest for any dishonest merchant today. Scripture elsewhere insists that crops fail for the righteous as well, and the passage should not be read as a law of cause and effect for every field and every shop.

Verse 8, however, is clearly meant to carry forward. It is addressed to 'O man,' adam, which widens the audience to every person, and it describes the shape of faithful life for anyone who belongs to God. The offerings of verses 6 and 7 are described in order to be refused, and child sacrifice is condemned throughout Scripture. The believer's use of the passage is to hold worship and ethics together: worship that does not issue in honest dealing and kindness is unacceptable, and honest dealing that has no relation to the God who redeemed us is incomplete. It is not a licence to abandon worship, since the same LORD who is displeased with empty sacrifice is the one who commands the offerings in the first place.

debates.question: Does Micah 6:8 teach that we are saved by doing justice, mercy, and humility?

views.label: The shape of covenant life, not a way to earn salvation
views.case: Micah addresses a people already redeemed from Egypt by grace, verse 4; verse 8 describes the life that flows from redemption, the response God has always wanted, not a ladder by which sinners climb to God. Deuteronomy 10:12 to 13 stands in the same covenant frame.

views.label: A moral summary that exposes our need
views.case: Read alongside the whole book, the verse also functions to expose how far short all people fall, driving them to the mercy and pardon that only God provides, fulfilled in Christ at 7:18 to 20. Titus 3:5 says that we are saved not by righteous deeds but according to His mercy.

debates.bearing: Both readings guard against turning verse 8 into works-righteousness: it is the good life God requires, which no one perfectly renders, and which sends us to the Redeemer who both fulfills it and pardons our failure.

debates.question: Is the offer of the firstborn in verse 7 a real possibility or a rhetorical climax?

views.label: A real practice that Judah was tempted by
views.case: Child sacrifice was actually practiced in Judah. Ahaz sacrificed his son in the fire, 2 Kings 16:3, and Manasseh did the same, 2 Kings 21:6, and Jeremiah 7:31 says the LORD never commanded it. On this reading the worshiper is raising a live option, and Micah is rejecting it explicitly.

views.label: The top step of an escalating rhetorical series
views.case: The sequence runs from calves to thousands of rams to ten thousand rivers of oil, numbers no one could afford, so the firstborn may simply be the final, most extravagant offer in a list of absurd bids. The point is the absurdity of trying to purchase favor.

debates.bearing: The two readings land in the same place: no gift, however extravagant or costly, can substitute for the life of justice, mercy and humility, and the God who stopped Abraham's hand, Genesis 22:12, does not want the child.

study.originalLanguages:
The summons of verse 2 uses the word for a lawsuit, rib, which is the legal action of one party against another. Hosea 4:1 uses it of the LORD's case against the people of the land, and Jeremiah 2:9 uses the matching verb, 'I will contend with you.' The mountains and hills as witnesses are not decoration; they are the enduring foundations of the earth, in verse 2's words, which have been there since the covenant was made and can testify to its terms.

The verb in verse 5, 'acknowledge,' is the verb of knowing, and what is to be known is 'the righteousness of the LORD.' The Hebrew noun here is a plural, which is why it is often read as the LORD's righteous acts. The exodus, the sparing of Israel from Balaam's curse and the crossing of the Jordan are acts in which the LORD showed Himself in the right. Remembering them is meant to bring the people to the verdict that He has done them no wrong.

The three clauses of verse 8 are built with careful verbs. The first, 'to act justly,' is literally to do mishpat, the same justice that the leaders of chapter 3 failed to know and love. It is an action, not a feeling. The second, 'to love mercy,' uses the verb of love with the noun chesed, the word for loyal, covenant-keeping devotion that the BSB renders 'loving devotion' in Micah 7:18 when it says the LORD delights in it. The text does not tell people merely to show mercy but to love it, so that it is an attachment and not a duty. The third, 'to walk humbly with your God,' joins a rare verb for lowliness with the verb 'to walk.' Proverbs 11:2 has a related word, 'with humility comes wisdom.' Walking with God is the language of Enoch, Genesis 5:24, and of Noah, Genesis 6:9, and it names a life lived in constant company.

The opening of verse 8, 'He has shown you,' is a perfect verb, a completed act. God has already disclosed what is good, so the people cannot plead ignorance. And the word 'require' is the verb for seeking, so the sense is 'what is the LORD seeking from you?' It has the sound of a God who wants something and not a clerk who exacts a price.

Verse 9 is notoriously difficult in Hebrew, and the BSB's parenthetical 'it is sound wisdom to fear Your name' is one way of handling an obscure phrase. The main command, 'Heed the rod and the One who ordained it,' is clear: the coming judgment has a Sender.

The BSB footnote on verse 16 observes that the Septuagint reads 'the scorn of the nations' where the Hebrew has 'the scorn of My people.' The two readings differ in who is scorned and by whom, and the BSB follows the Septuagint. Either way the verse ends with the city made a desolation, an object of contempt.

typology.type: The firstborn offered for the sin of the soul, Micah 6:7
typology.fulfillment: The worshiper asks whether he should give his firstborn for his transgression. The Bible's answer comes in two stages. First, God stopped Abraham's hand and provided a substitute, Genesis 22:12 to 14. Then He gave His own Son: 'He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32. The question that the worshiper cannot answer is answered by the sacrifice God Himself provides. The type falls short because the worshiper's offer is human and fearful, whereas God's gift is willing and sufficient.

The multiplication of offerings cannot please God, and Hebrews shows why: sacrifices and burnt offerings were never the final thing He wanted, and Christ says 'I have come to do Your will, O God,' Hebrews 10:5 to 9. His one offering accomplishes what thousands of rams could not, Hebrews 9:14. The correspondence is real, but it is an escalation, since the old offerings were a shadow and Christ is the substance, so the question 'with what shall I come before the LORD?' has the answer 'through Him.'

typology.type: One who walks humbly with God, Micah 6:8
typology.fulfillment: Enoch and Noah walked with God, but the One who fully walks in humility is Christ, who 'humbled Himself and became obedient to death,' Philippians 2:8. He did justice, loved mercy and was among us as one who serves. The type falls short because the figures of the Old Testament walked humbly in part, and Christ does it perfectly, so that He fulfills for His people what verse 8 requires and then forms the same life in them.

typology.type: The lawsuit and the sentence, Micah 6:2 and 6:13 to 16
typology.fulfillment: The covenant lawsuit of the prophets finds its culmination in the cross, where the sentence of the covenant falls on the faithful Israelite in place of the guilty. Where the people's curse was to eat and not be satisfied, Christ takes the curse so that believers may be satisfied, as He promises the hungry in Luke 6:21. The correspondence is not a direct prediction but a pattern: the LORD's case ends in a judgment that someone must bear.

study.christ:
Micah 6 leads to Christ by showing a question that only He can answer. 'With what shall I come before the LORD?' is the oldest question of religion, and the chapter's answers are all insufficient. Calves, rams and oil cannot do it. Even the firstborn cannot pay for the sin of the soul. The question is not foolish; it is correct, and it is unanswerable by human resources.

The New Testament answers it in two moves. First, it says God has already given the thing the worshiper offers in desperation: He 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32, and so the sacrifice of a firstborn is made by God and not by us. Second, it says the Son makes the offering that the whole system pointed toward. Hebrews quotes the psalm in which sacrifice and offering are not what God desired, and says Christ came to do His will, Hebrews 10:5 to 9, and that through the eternal Spirit He offered Himself unblemished to God, Hebrews 9:14.

Christ is also the one who lives out verse 8 in full. He did justice: He proclaimed good news to the poor and release to the oppressed, Luke 4:18, and defended the widow and the outsider. He loved mercy: 'go and learn what this means: I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' He told the religious leaders, Matthew 9:13, in explaining why He ate with sinners. He walked humbly with God: He emptied Himself, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death on a cross, Philippians 2:7 to 8. Jesus names the same three things when He says that the Pharisees tithe herbs but neglect justice, mercy and faithfulness, Matthew 23:23.

The covenant lawsuit also leads to the cross. The prophets' charge was that the LORD's people had broken His covenant and deserved the curses written in it, verses 13 to 16. At the cross the curse falls on the one who had not broken it, and the way is opened for the very thing verse 8 asks, a life of justice, mercy and humility, now empowered by mercy that has already been given. 'He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy,' Titus 3:5.

A caution: Micah 6:8 is not a messianic prophecy in the sense of 5:2. The link to Christ is through the way the New Testament takes up the same themes, and through the fact that Christ alone does and satisfies what the verse requires.
study.god:
Micah 6 begins with a God who does something rare in the Old Testament: He argues. The LORD of the covenant does not simply command; He invites His people to bring a complaint against Him. 'What have I done to you? Testify against Me,' verse 3. He opens Himself to cross-examination because His record is clean. This shows a God who takes relationship seriously, who gives reasons and who treats His people as persons who can be addressed and not merely subjects who must be silenced.

He is shown as a God who redeems before He requires. Verse 4 begins with what He did: 'I brought you up from the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery.' The obligation of verse 8 is built on a gift. He is the God of Exodus, who sent leaders, turned Balaam's curse into blessing, and brought the people across the Jordan. His acts are called 'righteousness' in verse 5, which means that His faithfulness shows itself in deliverance, and any demand He makes comes after a rescue.

He is shown as a God who cannot be bought. The escalation of verses 6 and 7 fails because the God addressed is not enriched by gifts. Psalm 50 and Isaiah 1 both make the same point, that He does not need bulls or rams. And He is shown to hate the very thing the worshiper offers as the ultimate price, since child sacrifice is something that never entered His mind, Jeremiah 7:31.

He is a God whose character is the content of what He requires. Justice, mercy and walking humbly are not arbitrary tests but a picture of Himself. He is the God who does justice for the fatherless and widow, who loves loyal devotion, and who walks among His people. To ask this of them is to ask them to be like Him.

He is also a God who judges what He has called. The final verses show that He hears the lies and measures the bags of false weights, and that the curses of the covenant are His own word. His justice is specific: it knows the short ephah. Yet the chapter opens with 'My people' and closes the case with a call to heed the rod and the One who ordained it. The sentence is meant to be heard.

For worship, the chapter says that God is not looking for more but for the right thing, and that He has already told us what that is.

crossReferences.note: Moses asks what the LORD requires of Israel and answers with fearing, walking in all His ways, loving Him, serving Him with all the heart and keeping the commandments. Micah 6:8 is the prophet's compressed form of the same question and answer, so the verse is not new teaching but a recall of the covenant's core.

The LORD says He desires mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. The word for mercy is chesed, the same word as in Micah 6:8. Hosea and Micah prophesied in the same century, and they together present a clear prophetic principle about what God wants beneath the ritual.

The LORD says He is full of burnt offerings and takes no delight in the blood of bulls, and then gives a list of what He does want: wash, cease doing evil, seek justice, defend the fatherless and plead for the widow. It is the longest prophetic commentary on Micah 6:6 to 8.

Samuel tells Saul that obedience is better than sacrifice and attentiveness better than the fat of rams. The principle that God values obedience above offerings was stated at the beginning of the monarchy, and Micah's question about thousands of rams is an echo of it centuries later.

David confesses that God does not delight in sacrifice or the burnt offering, but that a broken and contrite heart He will not despise. It is the penitent's side of Micah 6:8: humility is the posture in which a sinner approaches God, not an extra to be added after sacrifice.

Ahaz, a king of Judah during Micah's ministry, sacrificed his son in the fire like the nations before. It shows that the question 'Shall I present my firstborn?' was not hypothetical in Micah's day but touched a practice in the royal house.

God stops Abraham from laying a hand on Isaac and provides a substitute. The principle that God does not want the child is established at the start of Israel's story, and it also looks forward to the offering that God Himself will make, so that the question of Micah 6:7 is answered before it is asked.

Merchants long for the Sabbath to end so that they can reduce the ephah, increase the shekel and cheat with dishonest scales. The practice that Micah calls the short ephah in 6:10 and 11 was a recognizable feature of the age, and it shows that worship and trade had been separated.

Ahab did evil in the sight of the LORD more than all who were before him, built an altar for Baal and set up an Asherah pole. The 'house of Ahab' in Micah 6:16 is a recall of this record, and it tells Judah that the path they are on has an end that others have already walked.

Jesus says the scribes and Pharisees tithe mint, dill and cumin but neglect the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy and faithfulness. The echo of Micah 6:8 is plain, and it shows Christ reading the prophets as one with the Law and applying Micah's three requirements to His own day.

God did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all. It answers the question 'Shall I present my firstborn for my transgression?' in Micah 6:7: God makes the offering Himself, and He does it for our sin, so that those who could never pay are freely given all things.

Christ says that sacrifice and burnt offering God did not desire, and 'I have come to do Your will.' The passage takes Micah's argument about empty offerings to its completion, since the old system is taken away to establish the obedience that God wanted, and it is accomplished in Christ.

study.oneStory:
Micah 6 stands at the place in the biblical story where the covenant's terms are enforced. God had rescued Israel out of Egypt and given them a way of life at Sinai, and the whole arrangement was built on remembering what He had done and responding in kind. The lawsuit shows what happens when a redeemed people forget: they put religion in one pocket and commerce in another, and the LORD has to bring a case.

The chapter also answers a question as old as Eden. After Genesis 3 the question of how a sinful human being approaches God becomes the problem of religion. Cain offers the fruit of the ground and Abel the firstborn of the flock, Genesis 4:3 to 4, and ever since people have tried to find the right thing to bring. The book of Leviticus gives a divinely appointed set of offerings, but Micah's point is that no offering substitutes for a life that shares God's character, and no human offering can answer for sin.

What Micah shows he cannot give, the story supplies. In Genesis 22 God provides the substitute for Abraham's son. In Hebrews 10 Christ comes to do God's will. In Romans 8:32 the Father gives up His own Son. The cross is the answer to Micah 6:7, and it is why verse 8 can be a description of life and not an impossible burden: those who have been pardoned are re-formed by the Spirit to do justice, love mercy and walk humbly. In the next chapter Micah himself reaches the pardon, a God who pardons iniquity and delights in loving devotion, Micah 7:18.

The church then lives out verse 8 between the first and second coming. James says pure religion is to care for orphans and widows in their distress, James 1:27, and Hebrews says that a sacrifice of praise and the doing of good and sharing are what please God, Hebrews 13:15 to 16. Paul urges believers, because of God's mercy, to offer their bodies as living sacrifices, Romans 12:1.

The end of the story is a city where there are no false scales and no sentence. The curses of verses 14 and 15 are undone when 'no longer will there be any curse,' Revelation 22:3, and the hunger and thirst of those who ate without being satisfied are answered by a river of the water of life, Revelation 22:1, and a tree that yields fruit every month. Those who walk with God in the new creation will see His face, Revelation 22:4.

sermon.title: What God Requires
sermon.why: Begg preaches Micah 6:1-8, tracing God's covenant lawsuit and the futility of trying to satisfy Him with sacrifice, then unfolding what the LORD truly requires, to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with God, and showing that this life is grounded in and made possible by grace rather than a means of earning it.

quiz.q: What kind of scene does Micah 6 open with?

options.text: A covenant lawsuit, with God calling the mountains as witnesses and bringing a case against His people.
options.note: The prophets picture the broken covenant as a court case with creation as witness.

options.text: A coronation of the new king in Jerusalem.
options.note: There is a King in Micah, but chapter 6 is a courtroom, not a coronation.

options.text: A description of a festival with joyful sacrifices.
options.note: Sacrifices are mentioned, but to be relativized, not celebrated; the setting is a lawsuit.

options.text: A private vision with no reference to God's people.
options.note: God explicitly brings a case against His people, Israel.

quiz.q: How does God begin His case against His people in verses 3 to 5?

options.text: By asking what He has done wrong and recalling how He redeemed them from Egypt.
options.note: The wounded question, what have I done to you, rehearses His saving grace to move them to return.

options.text: By immediately listing every sin they have committed.
options.note: The charges come later; He opens with His own kindness and their ingratitude.

options.text: By threatening to destroy the mountains and hills.
options.note: The mountains are witnesses, not targets of the threat.

options.text: By denying that He had ever helped them at all.
options.note: He points precisely to His help: the exodus, Moses, Aaron, Miriam.

quiz.q: What does the LORD require, according to Micah 6:8?

options.text: To act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God.
options.note: This is the compact summary of the life God has always wanted from His redeemed people.

options.text: To bring ever larger and more costly sacrifices.
options.note: That is exactly what verses 6 and 7 pile up and verse 8 sets aside.

options.text: To fear the mountains and the foundations of the earth.
options.note: Creation is only the witness; the call is to walk humbly with God.

options.text: Nothing at all, since God asks for no response.
options.note: God clearly shows what is good and requires it of His people.

quiz.q: Why does God reject the offerings imagined in verses 6 and 7?

options.text: Because He wants a just, merciful, and humble heart, not ritual offered in place of it.
options.note: Even the extreme offer of the firstborn cannot substitute for a surrendered life.

options.text: Because burnt offerings were never part of Israel's worship.
options.note: Sacrifice was commanded; the problem is using it to avoid giving the heart.

options.text: Because the calves and rams were not valuable enough.
options.note: The issue is not the size of the gift but the state of the heart.

options.text: Because God is pleased by child sacrifice instead.
options.note: Child sacrifice is condemned; verse 7 exposes a heart that will give anything but itself.

quiz.q: How is this chapter answered in Christ?

options.text: He alone lived the justice, mercy, and humble walk God requires, and He is the firstborn given for our sin.
options.note: Christ fulfills 6:8 and answers the lawsuit no sinner could, giving the firstborn we could never give.

options.text: He taught that God no longer cares about justice or mercy.
options.note: Jesus intensifies these as the weightier matters of the law, Matthew 23:23.

options.text: He offered thousands of rams to satisfy God's case.
options.note: Christ offered Himself once for all, not the sacrifices verse 7 imagines.

options.text: He has no connection to the demands of this chapter.
options.note: Christ is both the fulfiller of 6:8 and the answer to God's lawsuit.

questions: God asks His people, what have I done to you? When you drift from God, does it help to remember His past kindness to you rather than only your failures?
The worshiper in verses 6 and 7 will offer anything except a changed heart. Where are you tempted to give God activity, money, or religion instead of yourself?
Micah 6:8 calls you to do justice. Where in your daily dealings, work, or money is God asking you to treat others rightly and refuse dishonest gain?
To love mercy is to delight in showing loyal kindness because you have received it. Who is God calling you to show mercy to this week?
To walk humbly with God is a whole life of dependence. What would it look like to trade self-reliance for a humble, daily walk with Him?

translationNotes.note: Shittim to Gilgal marks the last wilderness camp and the first camp in the promised land; the journey recalls God bringing Israel safely into Canaan. Shittim can also be rendered Acacia Grove.

To act justly, love mercy, and walk humbly renders three Hebrew phrases: do mishpat (justice), love chesed (steadfast, covenant mercy), and walk humbly (hatsnea lekhet), a whole life lived modestly and dependently with God.

The BSB follows the Septuagint reading you will bear the scorn of the nations; the Hebrew reads the scorn of My people. The statutes of Omri and the house of Ahab recall the wicked northern dynasty as the pattern Judah is condemned for following.
